plate_findings.evidence: Hepatopetal flow in the portal vein highly modulated by the cardiac cycle

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 4 panels (A, B, C, D). A: CT image showing cardiomegaly, which is listed in the text as a supportive finding for the diagnosis of congestive hepatopathy. B: Ultrasound image demonstrating a dilated suprahepatic vein, a sign of hepatic venous congestion associated with CH. C: Doppler ultrasound demonstrating dilation of a suprahepatic vein, supporting the diagnosis of CH. D: Doppler ultrasound capturing characteristic pulsatile flow in the portal vein, a sign of venous congestion and high pressure in CH.

in_text_mentions: Imaging tests help both to support the diagnosis of CH and to identify complications. It is of great help to specify the clinical suspicion of CH in the radiological request since many of the findings are elusive. Importantly, none of them is specific to CH and, therefore, the diagnosis should also be supported by other extrahepatic findings such as cardiomegaly, hypertrophy of the right atrium and ventricle, thickening and calcification of the pericardium, pericardial effusion, or pleural effusion [73] (Figure 2A).

e normal variation of their diameter with respiratory movements, loss of normal triphasic hepatic venous waveform (under physiological conditions the hepatic veins present a predominantly anterograde flow with a triphasic wave pattern, in which four waves can be identified—“a”, “S”, “v” and “D”, each corresponding to a different phase of the cardiac cycle), and increase in the portal vein pulsatility index and in hepatic arterial resistance [73,74] (Figure 2B–D). Of note, the appearance of a nodular or heterogeneous liver on standard imaging is not sufficient to diagnosis cirrhosis in CH [15].

plate_findings.evidence: Postmortem example of the classical “nutmeg” liver

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Panel A shows the gross, postmortem appearance of a nutmeg liver, which is a characteristic finding of congestive hepatopathy. B: Panel B displays histopathology showing centrilobular congestion and red blood cell extravasation, consistent with congestive hepatopathy. C: Panel C provides a higher magnification view of the centrilobular findings (congestion and RBC extravasation) seen in Panel B, supporting the diagnosis of congestive hepatopathy.

in_text_mentions: en characterized as a “nutmeg liver”, due to the presence of dark centrilobular zones that reflect sinusoidal congestion alternating with pale periportal zones with normal or fatty liver tissue [74] (Figure 5A). Characteristic histological findings include sinusoidal dilatation and congestion, hepatocyte atrophy most prominent in zone 3, extravasation of red blood cells into the space of Disse, regenerative hyperplasia emerging from periportal regions, and centrilobular fibrosis (Figure 5B,C) [67]. plate_findings.evidence: histological findings corresponding to the so called 'nutmeg pattern'

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 8 panels (Case 1a, Case 1b, Case 2a, Case 2b, Case 3a, Case 3b, Case 4a, Case 4b). Case 1a: Histopathology shows marked distortion and fibrotic bridging in Case 1, consistent with the target disease. Case 1b: Histopathology shows magnified view of fibrotic processes in Case 1, supporting the diagnosis. Case 2a: Histopathology confirms thicker centrilobular fibrosis and fibrotic bridging in Case 2. Case 2b: Histopathology confirms extensive fibrosis in Case 2, consistent with the disease. Case 3a: Histopathology shows liver architecture consistent with the known complications of the target disease. Case 3b: Histopathology demonstrates structural abnormalities in Case 3 characteristic of the target disease. Case 4a: Histopathology of Case 4 is noted to resemble the nutmeg pattern, linking it to the target disease. Case 4b: Histopathology of Case 4 shows fibrotic changes consistent with the mentioned nutmeg pattern.

panels.figure_caption: Liver histopathology obtained at autoptic examination by Masson’s Trichromic staining: (a) a panoramic view (×10 magnification) and (b) close up view (×40 magnification). In particular, the marked distortion of the liver structure, with fibrotic bridges arising from centrilobular veins and involving sinusoidal spaces and portal tracts, can be seen. Note the increasing thickness of fibrotic septa from Cases 1 to 4, so as to manifest the characteristic condition of “reverse cirrhosis”; moreover, in Case 4, the presence of cholestasis also resembles the so called “nutmeg pattern”.

panels.rationale: Whole-figure plate of 3 panels (A, B, C). A: Panel A provides direct measurement of dilated hepatic veins and IVC, which are key manifestations of hepatic venous congestion in congestive hepatopathy. B: Panel B shows spectral Doppler analysis revealing hemodynamic changes (loss of triphasic flow) highly suggestive of congestive hepatopathy. C: Panel C displays characteristic lobulated contours and the nutmeg appearance on CT, indicating chronic hepatic venous congestion.

panels.figure_caption: (A) The dilated hepatic vein (HV) lumen ranged from 12 to 18 mm in diameter. The intrahepatic inferior vena cava (IVC) was also dilated (31 mm in diameter; measurement not annotated in the image). (B) Spectral waveform analysis of the patient’s hepatic veins revealed the loss of a regular triphasic flow pattern, with an impression of a prominent a wave and v wave. These findings represent hemodynamic changes in the hepatic venous system that were highly suggestive of congestive hepatopathy. (C) Contrast-enhanced CT of the upper abdomen revealed lobulated liver contours and a “nutmeg” appearance of the parenchyma, which is indicative of chronic hepatic vein congestion.

in_text_mentions: A review of his vital sign chart did not reveal any episode of hypotension. An urgent abdominal CT demonstrated mild liver enlargement, inferior vena cava and hepatic vein dilatation, retrograde hepatic venous opacification shortly after intravenous contrast injection, and cardiac chamber enlargement (Figure 2, 3). The viral hepatitis panel was negative. On review of his medication chart remdesivir was considered the probable culprit and was discontinued two days after initiation. Given the CT and clinical findings, diuretic treatment was initiated.

in_text_mentions: A review of his vital sign chart did not reveal any episode of hypotension. An urgent abdominal CT demonstrated mild liver enlargement, inferior vena cava and hepatic vein dilatation, retrograde hepatic venous opacification shortly after intravenous contrast injection, and cardiac chamber enlargement (Figure 2, 3). The viral hepatitis panel was negative. On review of his medication chart remdesivir was considered the probable culprit and was discontinued two days after initiation. Given the CT and clinical findings, diuretic treatment was initiated.
